claims.text: The target material is a single-phase bcc refractory high-entropy alloy, exemplified by HfNbTaTiZr.
The random-solid-solution state has high lattice distortion and mass disorder.
The random-solid-solution state has low thermal conductivity dominated by phonon scattering.
Thermal annealing can evolve the target alloy from a random distribution to growing, percolating SRO clusters.
SRO can be driven to percolation while the target alloy remains single-phase.
SRO is thermodynamically stable and kinetic barriers to percolation are overcome between approximately 800 K and 1500 K.
An interatomic potential must capture strong interatomic interactions and force-constant variations in order to reproduce SRO formation and evolution.
Standard interatomic potentials do not adequately reproduce SRO evolution.
A machine-learning Moment Tensor Potential can be used to simulate SRO evolution in an RHEA.
A percolating SRO network creates a heterogeneous potential landscape containing regions with different phonon-scattering strengths.
Isolated SRO clusters act as phonon-scattering centers and reduce thermal conductivity.
Percolation of SRO clusters produces continuous, coherent, low-scattering pathways.
Coherent ordering in a percolating SRO network reduces effective mass-disorder scattering for selected phonon modes.
SRO percolation may cause a directional phonon-glass-to-phonon-crystal transition.
Thermal conductivity has a non-monotonic dependence on the SRO order parameter: it decreases below a critical percolation threshold and plateaus or increases above it.
The conductivity response above percolation deviates significantly from serial/parallel mixing, Matthiessen's rule, and effective-medium predictions.
Point-defect-scattering and simple effective-medium models predict a monotonic decrease in conductivity as SRO increases.
The critical threshold and conductivity-change magnitude depend strongly on the potential's accuracy in predicting SRO cluster size and connectivity.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to single-phase bcc RHEAs in which SRO actually percolates and excludes phase-separated or non-percolating systems.
A strictly monotonic conductivity decrease with increasing SRO, together with persistent non-percolation, is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that the hypothesis does not apply when SRO remains isolated, but the falsification rule treats persistent isolation of the clusters as evidence that falsifies the hypothesis. Non-percolation would instead place the experiment outside the stated applicability domain.
